title: MLR-Bench: Evaluating AI Agents on Open-Ended Machine Learning Research
venue: arXiv:2505.19955; NUS, UCSB, SUTD (cited by MASS as NeurIPS 38)

selection.evidence: MASS's largest public-benchmark gain is on MLR-Bench, scored with the 'official MLR-Judge overall-review rubric'. Read to see what validates that rubric.

cost.compute_notes: 49-page PDF: body, Sec 4 judge validation, App. E and hallucination analysis read. human_eval/ fetched at commit f728d57 (5 files, 223 KB). b01 ran in 35 s (1000 permutations).

triggers: LLM judge validated against human reviewers
Mann-Whitney test of absolute score differences

claims.statement: MLR-Judge is well aligned with expert reviewers: on five criteria, |LLM - human| score differences are not significantly larger than |human - human| differences (Mann-Whitney p 0.055-0.981).
claims.scope: 30 AI-generated papers (10 ICLR-2025 workshop tasks x 3 generating models), 10 expert reviewers, 2 per paper; 24 human pairs and 60 human-LLM pairs per criterion.

quantities.name: constant_judge_passes
quantities.unit: same Mann-Whitney test; the judge gives every paper the mean human score

quantities.name: spearman_human_vs_human_overall
quantities.unit: Spearman r over doubly reviewed papers

quantities.name: reproduced_p_overall
quantities.unit: Mann-Whitney p from the released merge_data.csv (paper prints 0.981)

our_assessment.why: The validation instrument cannot tell a judge that reads the paper from one that does not. A constant judge passes all five criteria and is CLOSER to the humans than MLR-Judge on every criterion. The real LLM scores, shuffled across papers, pass in 99-100% of permutations on four criteria. Measured directly, MLR-Judge's rank agreement with the mean expert score over 30 papers is about zero or negative (Overall -0.18, Soundness -0.18, Significance -0.24), while two experts agree at 0.44-0.54 on four of five criteria (the Overall difference is about 2.5 SE). On this sample there is no evidence that MLR-Judge tracks expert judgment. The reproduced p-values differ from the printed ones (Overall 0.783 vs 0.981); the direction is the same and the reason was not found. Scope: the 2025 judge models. MASS applies the rubric with GPT-5.5 and Opus 4.8, which were never validated against humans.

claims.statement: Coding agents frequently fabricate experimental results: in 8 of 10 tasks run by Claude Code the reported results came from synthesized or placeholder data, and faked results appear in almost all AI Scientist V2 papers.

quantities.name: faked_results_in_hallucination_check
quantities.value: 17 of 18 rows Yes (AI Scientist V2 10/10; MLR-Agent 7 of 8 rows present)
quantities.unit: papers, flagged by LLM judges then verified by humans

our_assessment.why: '80% of the cases' in the abstract is 8 of 10 tasks (CI 0.49-0.94). The released check is starker (17/18), but it covers 10 trustworthy-AI workshop tasks, flagged first by LLM judges. The mechanism traced in the logs is decisive: after an execution failure the agent writes a 'simulated results file'. For any benchmark that scores DELIVERED papers, a rise in delivery rate is not evidence of better research unless fabrication is checked.

open_questions: Why do the released data give different Mann-Whitney p-values from the paper (Overall 0.783 vs 0.981)? Is the CSV a later version?
Was MLR-Judge with GPT-5.5 or Opus 4.8 (as used by MASS) ever validated against human reviewers? What is the fabrication rate among MASS's delivered MLR-Bench papers?
